Title: Accuracy of prospective assessments of 4 large language model chatbot responses to patient questions about emergency care: Experimental comparative study
Output Feature: Quality of chatbot responses to common emergency care questions
Key Findings:
“We created 10 emergency care questions that we fed into the free-access versions of ChatGPT 3.5 (OpenAI), Google Bard, Bing AI Chat (Microsoft), and Claude AI (Anthropic) on November 26, 2023. Each response was graded by 5 board-certified emergency medicine (EM) faculty for 8 domains of percentage accuracy, presence of dangerous information, factual accuracy, clarity, completeness, understandability, source reliability, and source relevancy. We determined the correct, complete response to the 10 questions from reputable and scholarly emergency medical references. These were compiled by an EM resident physician.”
”Each of the 4 chatbots’ responses to the 10 clinical questions were scored across 8 domains by 5 EM faculty, for 400 assessments for each chatbot. Together, the 4 chatbots had the best performance in clarity and understandability (both 85%), intermediate performance in accuracy and completeness (both 50%), and poor performance (10%) for source relevance and reliability (mostly unreported). Chatbots contained dangerous information in 5% to 35% of responses, with no statistical difference between chatbots on this metric (P=.24). ChatGPT, Google Bard, and Claud AI had similar performances across 6 out of 8 domains. Only Bing AI performed better with more identified or relevant sources (40%; the others had 0%-10%). Flesch-Kincaid Reading level was 7.7-8.9 grade for all chatbots, except ChatGPT at 10.8, which were all too advanced for average emergency patients. Responses included both dangerous (eg, starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation with no pulse check) and generally inappropriate advice (eg, loosening the collar to improve breathing without evidence of airway compromise).”
”AI chatbots have important deficiencies for EM patient advice, despite their consistent performance. Advice for when to seek urgent or emergent care is frequently incomplete and inaccurate, and patients may be unaware of misinformation. Sources of information are not generally disclosed. Patients who use AI to guide their health care assume potential risks. The use of AI chatbots for health information should be subject to further research, refinement, and regulation. We strongly recommend proper medical consultation to prevent potential adverse outcomes. Finally, we call for further validation of scoring tools and the development of literature reporting guidelines.”

Basically, you should not use ChatGPT for emergency medical advice— this is proven in this study. Further, using commercially available generative AI does not pose a reliable solution to limited access to medical care, at the state evaluated in this study.
This study considered a comprehensive medical perspective; if the chatbot is going to replace the doctor, it can’t just be evaluated for accuracy. The authors considered:
  • accuracy
  • presence of dangerous information
  • clarity
  • completeness
  • understandability
  • source reliability
  • source relevancy

Title: Active takeover failure of aggressive drivers during partially automated driving
Output Feature: If aggressive driving tendencies correlate to passive takeover failure
Key Findings:
“Given that aggressive driving attitudes may influence drivers’ risk-related decision-making, this study aims to explore whether active takeover failures involve drivers’ subjective intentions and their relation to aggressive preferences.”
”These findings suggest the necessity of judicial assessment of drivers’ subjective intent in cases of deliberate non-takeover at the legal level, enhanced behavioral management of “suspected crashfor-cash” drivers in insurance practices, and optimization of active safety technologies in automated driving system design to ensure road safety.”
”This demonstrates that drivers’ driving styles exhibit cross-situational consistency; they are more likely to maintain their usual driving style rather than be influenced by the style of the automated driving system. At the same time, non-aggressive drivers did not show this problem. These results highlight the importance of addressing road safety issues for aggressive drivers, especially in competitive takeover scenarios. On one hand, more advanced safety technologies are needed, including systems that monitor driver status in real time and take corrective action when driver errors occur. On the other hand, strengthening laws and regulations and tightening the supervision of aggressive driving are crucial to curbing the spread of such behaviors. Additionally, targeted training programs can help aggressive drivers adjust their behavior and reduce safety risks.”
